intro: Prague protects its old trees the same way it protects buildings: since 1992, national law lets the city legally register individual specimens as pamatne stromy, memorial trees, each with its own protection order and a fineable offence for damaging one. Roughly 200 trees currently hold that status across the city. Most of what follows are London planes planted in aristocratic gardens two centuries ago, alongside a monastery ash, an island oak tamed by imperial flood engineers, and a beech that split into two trunks on a 17th century battlefield. All of them are free to visit.
meta_description: Prague protects its old trees by law. 30 remarkable trees, from a disputed-age plane by the Lennon Wall to a 45-metre beech on a 1620 battlefield.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Prague that anyone can actually go and see is the Beethoven Plane, a London plane growing in the garden of the Grand Priory Palace on Velkoprevorske namesti in Mala Strana, estimated at somewhere between 200 and 300 years old. Its exact planting date is disputed, but its trunk, seven and a half metres around, is the thickest of any protected tree in the city, and it towers over the wall where tourists photograph the Lennon Wall without ever looking up.
question_meta: Prague's oldest visitable tree is a 200-300 year old plane by the Lennon Wall. Where it stands, and twenty-nine more remarkable trees.
question_context: Prague has an older tree than this one, but nobody can visit it. Dub Karel, a 550 year old oak in a private castle park at Kolodeje, is Prague's oldest tree by a wide margin, and its own official record calls it the most massive tree in the city. The land is privately owned and closed to visitors, so per this site's rule on withheld locations it is left off the list rather than published as a destination nobody can reach. That leaves the Beethoven Plane as the oldest tree anyone can actually walk up to. It grows in the garden of the Grand Priory Palace, once the Prague seat of the Order of Malta, on Velkoprevorske namesti in Mala Strana, its trunk towering above the same wall famous today as the Lennon Wall. The romantic story, that a young Beethoven sat dreaming beneath it during his 1796 visit, does not survive contact with the calendar: he was in Prague in February, an unlikely month for garden reveries. Its real age is disputed among Czech sources, ranging from around 200 to nearly 300 years, but no other protected tree in the city comes close to its girth.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Prague?
faq.a: The oldest tree anyone can visit is the Beethoven Plane in the Grand Priory Garden, Mala Strana, estimated at 200 to 300 years old depending on the source. An older oak exists at a private castle park in Kolodeje but sits on land closed to the public, so it is not published here.

faq.q: Are Prague's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: Every tree on this list are free to see. They stand in public parks, city gardens and one nature reserve, and none require an admission ticket.

A legally protected memorial tree, a status Czech law has allowed since 1992 for specimens of exceptional age, size or value. Prague currently has roughly 200 of them, each individually registered with its own protection order.

faq.q: Why does Prague have so many old plane trees?
faq.a: London planes were a fashionable, hardy choice for aristocratic and monastery gardens across Central Europe from the late 1700s on, and several of the trees planted then in Prague's palace and island gardens are still standing. Six of them made this list.

trees.name: The Beethoven Plane

location.address: Grand Priory Garden, Velkoprevorske namesti, 118 00 Praha 1

trees.story: The thickest protected tree in Prague has a trunk seven and a half metres around, and its most famous story is almost certainly false. Local guides say Ludwig van Beethoven rested beneath this plane during his 1796 visit to Prague, dreaming of a 19 year old countess while lodging at the nearby Golden Unicorn inn. He was in the city in February. Prague historians point out that picturing a composer dreamily sitting under a bare tree in midwinter is more charming than credible. What is verified is the trunk itself: 752 centimetres around as of 2013, up from 670 in 1996. It grows in the garden of the Grand Priory Palace on Velkoprevorske namesti, towering over the wall that has carried John Lennon graffiti since the 1980s, tall enough that most people photographing the Lennon Wall never look up to notice the tree that shades it. Its exact age is disputed: the Order of Malta's own legend claims the 12th century, which is botanically impossible since this hybrid plane did not exist before 1700, while official records put the planting between 1725 and around 1810. Either way it is very likely the oldest plane tree, and the most massive protected tree of any species, in Prague.
trees.access: Free; the tree towers above the public Grand Priory Garden wall on Velkoprevorske namesti and is visible from the square by the Lennon Wall at all times. The garden itself, used by the Artiseme design gallery, may keep separate hours to enter directly.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Malostranska tram and metro stop, via the Lennon Wall on Velkoprevorske namesti
trees.notes: Registered as Naturdenkmal-equivalent pamatny strom (registry 104326), protected since 30 July 1998. Age is genuinely disputed across sources: Czech Wikipedia cites a circa-1810 estimate from the national protected-tree register (USOP) alongside a documented 1725-1727 Baroque garden renovation as the more likely planting window; one secondary tourism source claims 290 years, which would push planting closer to 1735. Stated here as a wide, honest range (200-300) rather than a single false-precision number. The Beethoven anecdote is explicitly debunked by both primary sources as implausible given the February timing of his 1796 Prague visit.
trees.how_to_recognise: Towering over the Grand Priory Garden wall on the square by the Lennon Wall, 7.28 metres round, the thickest protected trunk in Prague.

trees.name: The Plane of Karlovo namesti

location.address: Park na Karlove namesti, 128 00 Praha 2

trees.story: Prague's most photographed memorial tree earned an unprintable nickname for the shape of one branch. The plane at Karlovo namesti sends a limb down toward the ground before it curls back upward, a silhouette locals have joked about for decades. Planted before the square was landscaped into a public park in 1876, the tree is Prague's most recognisable protected tree, with a trunk measured at nearly eight metres around in 2004 and a crown that spreads across the western half of the park. It has not had an easy two centuries. Restorers opened and cleaned a large cavity in its trunk in 1985, propped up the low branch responsible for its nickname, and in 2013 ringed the whole tree in a fence after years of visitors climbing on the very limb they came to look at. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 7 October 1998 for its growth, age and value as a specimen. Estimates for its exact age disagree, ranging from about 160 to 190 years depending on the source, which would put its planting somewhere between the early 1800s and the 1860s. Nobody has found a planting record to settle it.
trees.access: Free, public park (Park na Karlove namesti), open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Karlovo namesti metro station (Line B)
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom, protected since 7 October 1998. Girth (795 cm, 2004) and height (17 m, 2009) are confirmed by two independent sources. Age is flagged because sources disagree meaningfully: one gives a maximum estimate of 160-170 years, Czech Wikipedia gives approximately 190 years; stated here as the full 160-190 range rather than picking one.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the park on the square, 7.14 metres round, with one limb that dips toward the ground before curling back up, which is what the nickname is about.

trees.name: The Plane of Kinsky Garden

location.address: Kinskeho zahrada, near the entrance from Kinskeho namesti, 150 00 Praha 5

trees.story: The largest tree on all of Petrin hill also lost its own sculpture to theft. In 1928 the sculptor Karel Dvorak placed a statue called The Fourteen Year Old at the foot of this plane in Kinsky Garden, and at some point in the following decades it disappeared. It now sits in a Prague City Museum storeroom, with a replacement reportedly still planned. The tree itself needed no help to become a landmark: at 28 metres tall with a trunk 546 centimetres around, it is visibly larger than anything else growing across the whole of Petrin, a hill covered in parks. It was planted during the first phase of the garden's construction, which ran until 1836, under a design by the Viennese architect Heinrich Koch for the Kinsky family, and Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 30 July 1998 for its growth, age and dendrological value. In 2004 it was one of thirteen Prague trees chosen for a genetic preservation programme that collects material from the city's oldest specimens before disease or storms can take them. For now it still shades the lower, flatter part of the garden nearest the entrance from Kinskeho namesti, exactly where it has stood for close to two centuries.
trees.access: Free, public garden (Kinskeho zahrada), open daily
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Svandovo divadlo tram stop, entrance from Kinskeho namesti
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom, protected since 30 July 1998. Girth (546 cm) and height (28 m) confirmed by two independent sources. Age given as an estimated 180-200 year range: one source states an estimated 180 years, while the documented planting window (1825-1836) implies closer to 190-200 by 2026; both are plausible and not a real contradiction, so the wider range is used rather than a single figure.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the lower flat part of the garden nearest the Kinskeho namesti entrance, 5.8 metres round, and the largest tree on the whole of Petrin hill.

trees.name: The Plane of Kampa

location.address: Kampa Park, northern edge near the Liechtenstein Palace entrance, 118 00 Praha 1

trees.story: A countess planted this tree in 1813 to dress up her family's riverside garden with something exotic, and it has outgrown every other reason anyone remembers her. Barbora Kolowratova Krakovska had the grounds beside the Vltava planted with foreign flowers and trees that year, and this plane is the clearest survivor of her garden, now absorbed into Kampa Park. It reaches 35 metres, taller than most buildings on the island, with a trunk 504 centimetres around, and it anchors the northern end of the park right where visitors enter from beside the Liechtenstein Palace. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 8 October 1998. Its exact planting date is one of the more solid facts on this list. Most of Prague's old plane trees carry an estimated age with a decade or two of margin either side; this one has a year, because someone wrote it down at the time. Kampa itself was still gardens and orchards when the tree went in, well over a century before the 1947 to 1948 landscaping that turned the island into the public park it is today, which means the tree predates the park built around it by more than a hundred years.
trees.access: Free, public park (Kampa Park), open at all times
trees.transport: 3 min walk from Malostranska tram and metro stop, via the steps down to Kampa near Charles Bridge
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 104322/11122), protected since 8 October 1998. Planting year (1813) and planter (Barbora Kolowratova-Krakovska) are documented and consistent across both sources, unusually precise for a Prague memorial tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: At the northern edge of the park near the Liechtenstein Palace entrance, 5.06 metres round, and the one Prague plane that carries a planting year rather than an estimate.

trees.name: The Twin Beech of Hvezda

best_time.label: late October, when the canopy of Central Europe's tallest tree on this list turns copper

location.address: Obora Hvezda nature reserve, near Brevnovska brana, 162 00 Praha 6-Liboc

trees.story: One of the two tallest trees on this page stands on a 17th century battlefield and splits into two trunks a few feet off the ground, which is why it is simply named Twin Beech. At 45 metres it beats every other tree here for height by a wide margin, in the Star Game Reserve on Prague's western edge, where the armies of the Bohemian Revolt collided with the Habsburgs in 1620. The beech itself came generations later, planted sometime after 1763, when the reserve was restored and replanted with beeches, oaks and hornbeams following decades of neglect. Its trunk, 508 centimetres around where it forks, now carries a binding to keep the two main stems from splitting apart under their own weight, and a wooden fence around its base, installed after years of visitors carving initials and hearts into the bark. Prague declared it a protected natural monument on 22 August 2001. It stands about 170 metres from the reserve's Brevnov Gate, in sight of the star shaped Renaissance hunting lodge the whole park is named for, a building that has watched over this beech's entire two and a half centuries of growth without ageing anywhere near as gracefully itself.
trees.access: Free, public nature reserve (Obora Hvezda)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Obora Hvezda or Vypich tram and bus stops
trees.notes: Registered natural monument (registry 104290), protected since 22 August 2001. Girth (507-508 cm) and height (45 m) confirmed by two independent sources. Age estimates range from 210 to 250 years across two assessments (2016 and 2019); midpoint of roughly 230 used as the headline estimate with the full range preserved in age_min/age_max.
trees.how_to_recognise: About 170 metres in from the Brevnov Gate, splitting into two trunks a few feet off the ground, and at 45 metres the tallest tree on this page by a wide margin.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Stromovka

location.address: Kralovska obora (Stromovka), near the Mistodrzitelsky letohradek, 170 00 Praha 7-Bubenec

trees.story: Two very different ages have been written down for this tree, 80 years apart, and nobody has reconciled them. One record dates its planting to around 1804, from the earliest landscaping of the royal nursery here under the gardener Fuchs. A separate 2016 assessment put its age at only around 130 years. Both figures come from people who study this specific tree, and the gap between them is wide enough that this page states the honest range rather than pick a side: somewhere between 140 and 220 years old. What is not in dispute is the tree itself, a male ginkgo with a trunk 362 centimetres around and a crown 16 metres wide, growing near the old Mistodrzitelsky letohradek, the former Governor's Summer House, in a corner of Stromovka that used to be a nursery bed. Ginkgos are sometimes called living fossils because the species has barely changed in over 200 million years, and this one is among the oldest specimens in the Czech Republic regardless of which age estimate is correct. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree in 2004. Every November its fan shaped leaves turn a single uniform gold and drop within days, the trick every ginkgo performs.
trees.access: Free, public park (Stromovka / Kralovska obora)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Vystaviste tram stop, within Stromovka park near the Governor's Summer House

best_time.label: November, when its fan-shaped leaves turn gold and drop within days

trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom, formally declared 16 July 2004. Age is flagged because two sources genuinely disagree by roughly 80 years: a circa-1804 planting estimate tied to the original nursery landscaping versus a 2016 assessment of approximately 130 years. Stated as a wide honest range (140-220) rather than a false-precision single figure. Girth (362 cm) and crown width (16 m) are consistent across sources.
trees.how_to_recognise: Near the governor's summerhouse, 3.65 metres round, with fan-shaped leaves that turn one uniform gold and drop within days each November.

trees.name: The Oak of Cisarsky ostrov

location.address: Cisarsky (Trojsky) ostrov, embankment road, 170 00 Praha 7-Bubenec

trees.story: Prague's very first legally protected oak grows on an island that used to flood every spring until imperial engineers tamed it. Cisarsky ostrov, Emperor's Island, took its name from Habsburg era work to control the Vltava, and this pedunculate oak has stood on its embankment road since sometime in the early 1800s, watching barges pass on the navigation canal beside it rather than the river itself. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 26 October 1994, the first oak in the city to receive that status, ahead of every other oak now on this list. Its trunk splits into branches unusually low, at just a metre and a half up, and the crown that results spreads wider than the tree is tall, a shape typical of an oak that grew alone in open ground rather than crowded by a forest. A 2013 measurement put the girth at 457 centimetres, and the tree is estimated at around 190 to 200 years old, above average for its age and size according to the city's own survey. It stands about 200 metres from the footbridge that connects the island to Stromovka, on a quiet embankment road most visitors to the park next door never think to cross.

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.access: Free, public riverside path on Cisarsky ostrov
trees.transport: Bus 112 to the Kovarna stop, then a short walk along the island embankment; or cross the footbridge from Stromovka
trees.notes: Registered as Prague's first pamatny dub (memorial oak), protected since 26 October 1994 (registry 104336/11136). Girth (457 cm, 2013 measurement) and the 190-200 year age estimate are consistent across both sources.
trees.verify_notes: Reader feedback (via /contribute, 2026-08-15) flagged the location as wrong, no detail given. Re-checked 2026-08-23: Czech Wikipedia gives an explicit GPS citation, 50.1112953N 14.4137611E, matching our stored pin (50.1113,14.4138) almost exactly; prazskestromy.cz's descriptive location (southern shore path by the canal, under 200m from the Stromovka footbridge) also matches our story text. No error found against either source; outcome recorded as holds.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the island's embankment road, about 200 metres from the footbridge across to Stromovka, 4.78 metres round.

trees.name: The Ash of Strahov Garden

location.address: Velka strahovska zahrada, south of Uvoz street, 118 00 Praha 1-Hradcany

trees.story: The tallest single trunk on this page grows in the one corner of Strahov Monastery the monks decided to share. This ash reaches 37 metres in the Great Strahov Garden, the only part of the monastery complex left open to the public; the rest remains cloistered grounds. It began as an orchard tree in a working fruit garden, planted around the turn of the 19th century, long before anyone thought to protect it. Its trunk splits into three thick limbs about two metres above the ground and keeps climbing, measuring 513 centimetres around at the split as of a 2013 survey, a girth that puts it among the most massive ash trees recorded anywhere in the Czech Republic. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 13 October 2007. From the garden beneath it, visitors get one of the better free views in the city, Prague Castle and the rooftops of Mala Strana laid out below the hill, a vista the tree has been growing tall enough to share in for two centuries. At an estimated 210 to 230 years old, it was already well established when the garden's monastic orchard still supplied the friars with fruit rather than a footpath for tourists.
trees.access: Free, public garden (Velka strahovska zahrada), the only part of the Strahov Monastery grounds open to visitors
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Pohorelec tram stop (lines 22, 23)
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 105072/12762), protected since 13 October 2007. Girth (510-513 cm across 2007 and 2013 measurements) and height (37 m) are consistent across both sources.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the Great Strahov Garden, the one part of the monastery grounds left open to the public, 5.3 metres round and 37 metres up above the view over Mala Strana.

trees.name: The Field Maple of the Seminary Garden

location.address: Seminarska zahrada, above the pond below Petrinske terasy, 118 00 Praha 1

trees.story: Field maples are usually shrubs. Left alone, most stay a scrubby hedge tree, rarely climbing past a few metres. This one, in the Seminary Garden on Petrin's eastern slope, ignored the script and grew into a proper 24 metre tree, the only field maple in Prague to earn individual legal protection because of it. Its trunk measured 285 centimetres around in a 2013 survey, thick for a species whose Czech name, babyka, is usually attached to something closer to a bush. Prague declared it a protected memorial tree on 19 June 2009, and it stands above a small pond just below the Petrinske Terasy restaurant, roughly 250 metres north of the Nebozizek cable car stop, a stretch of the garden slightly off the paths most visitors to Petrin actually walk. At an estimated 160 to 170 years old, it has had more than enough time to prove it is the exception rather than the rule for its species. People who study field maples cite examples like this one as evidence the plant's usual shrub form is a matter of circumstance, not biology. Give it room, apparently, and a field maple will eventually decide to become a tree instead.
trees.access: Free, public garden (Seminarska zahrada)
trees.transport: 3 min walk from the Nebozizek funicular stop
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 105426/13166), protected since 19 June 2009. Girth (278-285 cm across 2008 and 2013 measurements), height (24 m) and the 2009 registration date are confirmed on the Czech Wikipedia article; the Wikidata entry corroborates the same registry numbers and species identification, but no independent narrative source was found beyond these two closely linked records, so this is flagged as thinner sourcing than the rest of the list despite the consistent data. Pin upgraded to confirmed 2026-07-27: this entry's own already-cited Wikidata item (Q26790033, specifically about this one tree) carries an individual P625 coordinate claim (50.083939, 14.399024) essentially identical to the stored pin, so the existing position is independently verified rather than a park-level estimate.
trees.how_to_recognise: Above the pond below the Petrin terraces, 2.93 metres round: a field maple grown to full tree size instead of staying the scrubby hedge shrub the species usually is.

trees.name: Neruda's Pear Tree

location.address: Seminarska zahrada, path crossing between Petrinske terasy and Hellichova street, 118 00 Praha 1

trees.story: This pear tree remembers a poet's birthplace that no longer exists. Jan Neruda, the 19th century writer whose name now marks Prague's most photographed street on the other side of the hill, was born in an army barracks that once stood near this spot on the eastern slope of Petrin; the barracks are long demolished, but the pear tree that stood nearby when he was a boy is still bearing fruit. Prague's tree survey estimates its age at around 190 years, measured a trunk 292 centimetres around in 2015, and calls it exceptionally old for its species, since wild pears rarely reach anywhere close to two centuries. Unlike most trees on this list, it carries no formal legal protection; the city added it to its inventory of significant trees only in 2013, one tier below the memorial tree status that comes with fines for damaging a tree. It grows at a quiet path crossing in the Seminary Garden, in the lower orchard section between the Petrinske Terasy restaurant and Hellichova street, a former monastery garden open to the public since 1930. Most visitors climbing Petrin for the views pass within a few metres of it without knowing an old pear tree, let alone one tied to Neruda, is there at all.
trees.access: Free, public garden (Seminarska zahrada), open since 1930
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Hellichova tram stop (lines 12, 20, 22), via the Seminary Garden entrance
trees.notes: Not a legally protected pamatny strom, only an entry in Prague's separate, lower-tier 'significant trees' inventory since 2013, unlike every other tree on this list. No exact coordinates were published in either source; location given here is approximate, triangulated from the described path crossing between Petrinske Terasy restaurant and Hellichova street within the Seminary Garden. Photo found 2026-07-28: iNaturalist observation 157617276 (CC BY, Dave Richardson, 29 April 2023), place_guess "Petrin Gardens, Prague 1", viewed directly and shows a gnarled old fruit-tree trunk in white blossom with young leaves, consistent with a wild pear in April; the observation's own coordinates sit roughly 200m from this entry's triangulated pin, close enough within the same garden to treat as the tree described here, though the pin itself stays approximate since the source only names a path crossing, not a survey point.

best_time.label: April, when it fills with white blossom before the leaves are fully out

trees.how_to_recognise: At a quiet path crossing in the lower orchard section, between the Petrinske Terasy restaurant and Hellichova street, and a fruiting pear rather than anything ornamental.

trees.name: The Oak of Dienzenhofer Gardens

location.address: Dienzenhoferovy sady, northeastern corner by V Botanice street, 150 00 Praha 5-Smichov

trees.story: The street on the far side of this oak is called V Botanice, In the Botanical Garden, and there is no botanical garden. Prague's tree register calls the oak the only living reminder of the one that used to be here, which makes a 160 year old tree the last exhibit of a collection nobody can visit. It stands at the northeastern corner of Dienzenhoferovy sady, a riverside strip of grass named after Kilian Ignac Dientzenhofer, the Baroque architect who put a pavilion on this ground in 1735. Traffic now runs on three sides of it, feeding the Jirasek Bridge, and the tree has answered the way open grown oaks do, by pushing its lowest limbs sideways instead of up until the crown measured 23 metres across in 2009 against a height of only 20. Its trunk has thickened from 350 centimetres in 2004 to 393 in 2017, which is a tree still laying on wood rather than holding station. Prague protected it on 17 February 2005. Surveyors keep recording its condition as very good, which for an oak marooned on a traffic island in a European capital is a small piece of luck.

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.access: Free, public park (Dienzenhoferovy sady), open at all times
trees.transport: 2 min walk from the Zborovska tram stop (lines 4, 5, 12, 15, 20), at the Jirasek Bridge end of the gardens
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 104828/12507), protected 17 February 2005. Two independent sources: the USOP-derived record (girth 350 cm in 2004, 375 in 2009, 378 in 2013; height 20 m; crown 23 m; age about 155 years as of 2018) and prazskestromy.cz, the Agentura Koniklec register (girth 378 cm in 2013, age about 160). The 2017 Koniklec printed map gives 393 cm, which is the figure used in the story as the most recent. The botanical-garden claim is the register's own and is stated as such rather than as established fact; the street name V Botanice corroborates that a garden stood here, nothing found dates it. Photo viewed at full size before approval: bright winter daylight, blue sky, the oak fills the frame with trunk and the whole spreading crown readable, and it holds the centre band of a wide card crop. It is leafless, which the Cadiz standard permits (only night shots and black-and-white are excluded) and which suits a tree whose low sideways limbs are the point. This is the same file the Czech Wikipedia article on this tree uses, so the identification is not a guess.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the northeastern corner by the street called V Botanice, 3.93 metres round, effectively marooned on a traffic island.

trees.name: The Red Oak of Shooters' Island

best_time.label: late October, when it goes scarlet weeks after the embankment limes have finished

location.address: Strelecky ostrov, central part of the northern half of the island, 110 00 Praha 1

trees.story: An American tree turns the best colour in central Prague, on an island where Bohemian archers used to practise. Strelecky ostrov, Shooters' Island, is named for the crossbow and longbow ranges that operated on it from the reign of Charles IV, and its northern half is now a lawn under big trees with the Vltava running past on both sides. The red oak in the middle of that half arrived from North America by way of the European nursery trade, and at 352 centimetres around it is the largest oak on the island and, by the city's own reckoning, the largest red oak in the centre of Prague. It was added to the register of significant trees in 2013 at an estimated 125 years, which places its planting close to the landscaping that converted a shooting ground into a public park. Red oaks do one thing better than any native Czech tree and they do it late: the leaves go scarlet and then deep rust through the second half of October, long after the limes on the embankment have given up. Thousands of people cross Most Legii directly above this tree every day. The staircase down to it is on the bridge itself.
trees.access: Free, public park on the island, reached by the staircase and lift from Most Legii or the ramp from the Smichov bank
trees.transport: 3 min from the Narodni divadlo tram stop (lines 2, 9, 17, 18, 22), then the stairs down from Most Legii
trees.notes: Not a pamatny strom: this is a vyznamny strom, Prague's second tier, entry number 18, registered 2013, the same tier as prg_010. Girth 350 cm measured 2015 (prazskestromy) and 352 cm in the 2017 Koniklec printed map. Flagged for two reasons. First, the age is a single register estimate of about 125 years with no second assessment found, so the range here is deliberately wide. Second, the pin is approximate: no source publishes coordinates and the tree is not mapped in OpenStreetMap, so the position is triangulated from the register's own wording, the central part of the northern half of the island, which is an area roughly 60 metres across. The city portal's revitalisation page is the independent corroboration for the tree's standing and for the 2013 reopening of the island; it also records that the two largest oaks in the northern part were put forward for heritage status by the project's tree commission. No photo of this specific tree found on Commons, Openverse or iNaturalist in this pass.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the lawn in the northern half of the island, directly below Most Legii. The staircase down to it is on the bridge itself.

trees.name: The Bonsai Ginkgo of Na Slupi

best_time.label: mid-November, when the low spreading crown goes yellow and lays a circle of leaves on the grass

location.address: Botanicka zahrada Prirodovedecke fakulty UK, by the greenhouse entrance, Na Slupi 16, 128 00 Praha 2

trees.story: A tree five metres tall with the trunk of one twice that height has been interfered with. The ginkgo by the greenhouse door in the Charles University botanical garden measures about 343 centimetres around at chest height and goes almost nowhere upward, spreading and drooping instead, and the accepted explanation is that somebody grew it in a barrel and pruned it like a bonsai for years before it was ever put in the ground. It carries its own cultivar name, 'Praga', probably descended from the weeping 'Pendula'. It went in around 1860 to 1870, which means it was standing here before the garden was laid out around it. Czech readers may know its outline without knowing the tree, because a ginkgo leaf is the emblem of Jaroslav Foglar's 1965 novel Stinadla se bouri and this specimen is the one usually credited with the idea, though the older ginkgo in Riegrovy sady has a claim too and Foglar never settled it. Prague listed it as a significant tree in 2013. In November the whole low crown turns one flat yellow and lets go inside a week, which on a tree this wide leaves a ring of leaves on the grass rather than a drift.
trees.access: Free, the outdoor garden of the university botanical garden is open daily with seasonal closing times; the greenhouses beside the tree are ticketed, the tree itself is not
trees.transport: 5 min walk from the Botanicka zahrada tram stop (lines 6, 18, 24), or 10 min south from Karlovo namesti metro (Line B)
trees.notes: Vyznamny strom number 5, registered 2013, not a pamatny strom. Two independent sources: prazskestromy.cz (Agentura Koniklec) gives 340 cm measured at 80 cm above ground in 2015 and an age of about 150, and the Prague 2 district encyclopedia gives 343 cm at 1 m, a height of only 5 m, a planting date of about 1860 to 1870 and an age of 155 to 160 as of 2021. A third figure of about 130 years circulates and is the outlier, hence the range used here. Flagged on the Foglar attribution, which both sources treat as a tradition rather than a documented fact and which the district encyclopedia explicitly offers alongside a rival candidate, the older ginkgo in Riegrovy sady; the story keeps that hedge rather than dropping it. The pin is the OpenStreetMap node named for this individual tree with its cultivar, 'Jinan dvoulalocny Praga', which agrees with the register's description of the position by the greenhouse entrance. Note this is Prague's second ginkgo on the page, the first being prg_006 in Stromovka, 4.5 km north; no size or age comparison between the two is made because neither source ranks them.
trees.how_to_recognise: By the greenhouse door, about 3.4 metres round and only five metres tall, spreading and drooping rather than rising, as though a much bigger tree had been cut off short.

trees.name: Masaryk's Lime

location.address: Masarykova vyhlidka, Horni Jeleni prikop below Lumbeho zahrada, 118 00 Praha 1-Hradcany

trees.story: A president picked a tree, and an architect built a terrace around it. Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, installed at Prague Castle from 1918, took to sitting on a bare rise above the Deer Moat under a lime already more than a century old, so he set Josip Plecnik, the Slovene architect he had put in charge of remaking the castle, to make the spot worth sitting in. Between 1922 and 1924 Plecnik terraced the slope in stone, planted it with vines and left the lime standing at the centre of a three quarter circle platform. Masaryk's own bench did not survive. Two stone ones now flank the tree, which the castle's own account puts at over 200 years old. Then the place disappeared: from 1948 the entire moat was a guarded military zone, shut for four decades, and it was Vaclav Havel who had it opened again, with the viewpoint restored in 1996. The trunk is the one thing the sources will not agree on, 249 centimetres in one survey and 349 in another, a gap too wide to split. The view is not in dispute. The Archbishop's Palace and the cathedral line up below you, from a bench under a tree, which is what the whole thing was built for.
trees.access: Free, but only when the Upper Deer Moat is open, usually April to October, roughly 10:00 to 18:00. The viewpoint itself sits inside the castle security perimeter and has been closed for stretches under different presidents; since 2021 it is reachable only from the Upper Deer Moat and not from Klarov. Check the castle's opening notices before making the walk for this tree alone.
trees.transport: 8 min walk from the Brusnice tram stop (lines 22, 23), entering the Upper Deer Moat and climbing Plecnik's double staircase
trees.notes: Vyznamny strom number 12, registered 2013. Two independent sources: the Czech Wikipedia article on the Masaryk viewpoint, which draws on the Prague Castle Administration's 1996 Plecnik monograph and describes the lime as over 200 years old standing between the two stone benches, and prazskestromy.cz, which gives about 200 years and a girth of 249 cm measured 2016. The 2017 Koniklec printed map gives 349 cm for the same tree, a 100 cm discrepancy that one of the two has to have got wrong; the story states both rather than choosing. Flagged mainly on access: the viewpoint has been alternately open and closed under successive presidents and is inside the castle security perimeter, so the access field warns rather than promises. Pin is approximate, the Nominatim node for Masarykova vyhlidka; the lime stands on the viewpoint platform, so the error is metres rather than hundreds of metres, but no per-tree coordinate is published. No usable photo of the tree found: the Commons images of this viewpoint are views out over Hradcany with the lime out of frame or backlit.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the terrace Plecnik built around it in the Upper Deer Moat, with a bench beneath it and the cathedral lined up below; the moat opens roughly April to October.

trees.name: The Elm of Ruzova Street

location.address: Ruzova 941/2, near Jindrisska, 110 00 Praha 1-Nove Mesto

trees.story: Most of Europe's big elms are dead, and this one is standing on a side street between Wenceslas Square and the main station. Dutch elm disease, a fungus carried between trees by bark beetles, went through the continent in two waves last century and removed elms so thoroughly that a mature one is now a curiosity rather than an ordinary sight. The elm at Ruzova 941/2 has lived through both waves and shows no sign of either. It is a European white elm, the species with lopsided leaves and papery seed discs that ripen in May, 23 metres tall with a trunk 335 centimetres around, growing on a scrap of ground that was a front garden before the block turned into offices and hotels. The crown fills the courtyard behind the railings and leans out over the pavement, which is where you stand to look at it. Prague gave it legal protection only on 15 April 2022, roughly 190 years into its life, having put a fence around its base the year before. Elms that shrug off the fungus are studied as possible parents for resistant stock, so this one may yet turn out to be useful as well as old.
trees.access: Free, visible and approachable from the public pavement on Ruzova; the small garden the tree stands in belongs to the building and is fenced, so this is a tree you look up at from the street rather than walk around
trees.transport: 4 min walk from Hlavni nadrazi metro (Line C) or the Jindrisska tram stop (lines 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 24)
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 106429), declared 15 April 2022, one of Prague's most recent. Girth 335 cm and height 23 m measured 2022; age about 190 years; health recorded as stable, excellent to good, with excellent to slightly reduced vitality. Flagged on sourcing: the second source is a Czech popular travel article rather than an independent survey, and it plainly rests on the same register data, so this entry is effectively single-sourced on the numbers even though the tree's existence, species and position are not in doubt. It adds the point about the tree having survived grafioza, which the register record supports by implication rather than by statement. No superlative is claimed here on purpose: the 2020 Koniklec map calls the elm in Michelsky les the only memorial elm in Prague, a claim made two years before this tree was protected, and the two should not be set against each other. Photos on Commons exist under Category:Jilm v Ruzove ulici but all six were viewed and every one is a street view in which the tree is small, partly hidden by buildings and off to one side, so none passes the Cadiz standard.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the side street between Wenceslas Square and the main station, 3.35 metres round, with a fence put around its base in 2021.

trees.name: The Old Town's Only Oak

location.address: Rasnovka, the small square in front of the city road authority building, 110 00 Praha 1-Stare Mesto

trees.story: The Old Town has exactly one legally protected oak and it grows on a corner nobody photographs. Rasnovka is a scrap of a square in the north of the Old Town behind the Convent of Saint Agnes, with the early Gothic church of the Holy Saviour on one side and the functionalist offices of the city's road authority on the other. The oak stands between them, planted around 1850, when this quarter was still mills, timber yards and river trade rather than a conservation area. It is a pedunculate oak, the ordinary Czech oak of field boundaries and village greens, doing the unusual thing of reaching 19 metres in the middle of a city block, and its trunk has gone from 299 centimetres in 2010 to 321 in 2017. Prague protected it on 24 March 2001, and the last survey found no damage worth recording. It is about six centuries younger than the church beside it and eighty years older than the office block, which is a fair summary of what it is doing there: the one living thing on the square that watched both of its neighbours turn up.

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.access: Free, small public square open at all times
trees.transport: 4 min walk from the Dlouha trida tram stop (lines 6, 8, 15, 26), or 8 min from Namesti Republiky metro (Line B)
trees.notes: Registered pamatny strom (registry 104300/11100), protected 24 March 2001. Two independent sources agree: girth 265 cm in 2000, 299 in 2010, 309 in 2013 and 321 in the 2017 Koniklec map; height 19 m with a 16 m crown; age about 165 years as of 2016 with a planting date of about 1850; condition rated excellent in 2010 with no visible damage. The claim that this is the only protected oak in the Old Town is the register's own and is a district-level claim, so it does not collide with the city page's existing claim that the Cisarsky ostrov oak (prg_007) was the first oak in Prague to be protected. Photo viewed at full size before approval: May 2021, sunlit, blue sky, the oak occupies most of the frame with the full crown and the base of the trunk both readable, and the tree holds the centre of the image so a wide card crop keeps it. A parked car sits at the lower left and does not intrude on the centre band.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the scrap of a square behind the Convent of Saint Agnes, between the Gothic church of the Holy Saviour and the road authority's offices, 3.21 metres round.

trees.name: The Plane of Nove Mlyny

location.address: corner of Nove Mlyny and Klimentska, opposite the Church of St Clement, 110 00 Praha 1

trees.story:
The London plane is an accident. It did not exist before the seventeenth century, when an oriental plane and an American one crossed somewhere in a European garden and produced a tree that turned out to be almost impossible to kill in a city.

That accident is why planes line so many European streets, and why one of them stands on the corner of Nové Mlýny and Klimentská, opposite the church of St Clement, in the quiet Petrská quarter a couple of streets back from the Vltava. Prague's register of protected trees measured its trunk at 342 centimetres in 2017, and it has been adding to that figure ever since, because planes grow quickly. The register's note claims nothing grander than what it is: a locally dominant tree, above the average of its kind in size and age, protected on that basis. No planting date has been published, and that single entry is the whole of the evidence.

Plane bark is why the species won the nineteenth century. It sheds in plates instead of thickening, carrying off a year of soot and grime with it, which kept planes alive in industrial cities that killed nearly everything else. The shedding leaves the familiar camouflage of cream, olive and grey, and it shows best in winter, when there is nothing on the branches to distract from it.
trees.access: Free, on a public street corner
verified_sources: Czech register of memorial trees (Pamatny strom), girth 342cm measured 2017
trees.verify_notes: 2026-08-30: reader submission #54 flagged that this tree has no photograph, which the page already shows as an honest gap. The submitter also filled in the form's location field with our own published address, which is not independent confirmation of the pin and must not be read as one. Nothing about the location changed. Outcome: holds; asked whether they have a photograph. Submitter's name deliberately not recorded here, per the standing rule that no sender is ever named in the data.
trees.transport: Petrska ctvrt, Nove Mesto; tram 3, 8 or 24 to Prazska trznice or Revolucni, short walk
trees.how_to_recognise: On the street corner opposite the Church of St Clement, 3.42 metres round, its bark shedding in plates of cream, olive and grey.

trees.name: The Elm of Zatory

location.address: Bus terminus at the south exit of Nadrazi Holesovice metro station (Praha 7, Holesovice)

trees.access: Free, standing on public ground at a bus turning circle beside the metro station
trees.transport: Nadrazi Holesovice metro station (line C), at the exit
trees.story:
An elm marks a bus terminus outside Nadrazi Holesovice, and it is the last thing standing from a street. Na Zatorach once ran through old Holesovice, cleared in stages from the 1950s into the late 1970s: first for a concrete plant, then for the railway yard, then for the metro station and bus depot that occupy the ground today. One house, kept for its old street number, and this elm are what is left of it.

Prague's register of significant trees measured the trunk at 2.26 metres round in 2016 and put the tree at about 180 years old that year, which puts it near 190 now. The write-ups behind that figure trace back to the same 2016 survey rather than to two separate measurements, so treat the age as an estimate carried from one source, not a settled fact.

The species explains why it is the one tree that made it. European white elm tolerates wet, disturbed ground better than most trees, which is exactly what a rail yard and a bus turning circle produce, and it carries more resistance to Dutch elm disease than the common elm that wiped out most of the continent's street elms in the twentieth century. It stands where a demolished neighbourhood ends and a metro line begins, four kilometres north of the old town, ringed by the bus turning circle that is now the closest thing Zatory has to an address.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its slender 2.26-metre trunk standing alone at a bus turning circle. It stands at the south exit of Nadrazi Holesovice metro station.

trees.name: The Hungarian Oak of Italska Street

location.address: Grounds of the Italska Street clinic (Poliklinika AGEL, formerly the Railway Hospital), entrance from Helenska street, 120 00 Praha 2

trees.access: Free; stands in the grounds of a public health clinic (Poliklinika AGEL, formerly the Zeleznicni/Railway Hospital) near its main entrance from Helenska street, the same kind of openly walkable institutional ground as a hospital garden. Not gated off from the public during opening hours.
trees.transport: Bus 135 to Na Smetance, or an 8 min walk from Muzeum metro (lines A, C)
trees.story:
This oak reached Italska Street before the hospital did. Quercus frainetto is a Balkan and southeast European tree rather than a Czech one, and this specimen went in with the original garden landscaping of the ground above the main railway station's tracks, well before the building it now shares a lawn with was put up.

Both sources measure it at 291 centimetres round, from a survey in 2013. Its age is the part that will not settle. The national register, quoted by Czech Wikipedia, gives about 140 years as of 2019. The Agentura Koniklec survey behind prazskestromy.cz says nearer 155. Read together that puts the tree somewhere between 145 and 170 years old, and nobody has offered anything to close the gap.

Prague listed it as a pamatny strom, a protected memorial tree, on 7 March 1998, and the state's assessors rate its condition very good. It is not the largest Hungarian oak in the city. Another registered one at Palata stands 24 metres tall with 335 centimetres of trunk, so this tree holds second place in a field of two.

It grows in the grounds of the Italska Street clinic, the former Railway Hospital, near the entrance from Helenska. The ground is not gated off during clinic hours, the same open institutional lawn as any hospital garden.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its 2.91-metre trunk on the open lawn of a hospital garden. It stands in the grounds of the Italska Street clinic, near the entrance from Helenska.

trees.name: The Oak of U Malvazinky

location.address: U Malvazinky, on the open ground between houses no. 28 and 30, 150 00 Praha 5-Smichov

trees.access: Standing on private land between two apartment buildings; not enterable. Czech Wikipedia states plainly that it is 'nepristupny, ale z ulice dobre viditelny' (inaccessible, but well visible from the street). The pin marks the tree itself, which fronts the public street U Malvazinky; view it from the pavement rather than approaching the trunk.
trees.transport: Bus stop Malvazinky (route 137), on U Malvazinky street
trees.story:
You cannot get to this oak, and you do not need to. It stands on private ground between two apartment buildings on U Malvazinky, and Czech Wikipedia says plainly what to expect: nepristupny, ale z ulice dobre viditelny. Inaccessible, but well visible from the street. Look at it from the pavement and leave the trunk alone. The register's coordinate marks the tree itself rather than a surveyed spot to stand, so expect to find your own angle from the road.

It went in around 1855, a survivor of the tree cover that grew on this Smichov slope before the houses did. When Prague protected it as a pamatny strom on 3 February 2001, its trunk measured 265 centimetres round. A 2013 survey found 281. Both sources put its age at about 160 years as of 2016, which makes it roughly 170 now, and the state rates its condition very good.

Its branches run long and low in most directions, the shape a tree takes when nothing crowds it early.

Two hundred metres east stood the Malvazinka estate. Its land became the Malvazinky cemetery in 1876 and, after 1948, a state sanatorium. The oak watched that whole sequence from the open ground between numbers 28 and 30, which is where it has stood the whole time.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long low branches running out in every direction, on the open ground between houses 28 and 30. Look at it from the pavement, because the ground itself is private.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Plane of Jezerka Park

location.address: Park Jezerka, between the Divadlo Na Jezerce theatre and the park pond, 140 00 Praha 4-Nusle

trees.access: Free, public park (Park Jezerka), open at all times
trees.transport: Bus stop Jezerka (route 188), at the park entrance
trees.story:
The park came second. This plane was planted around 1815, and Prague did not begin laying out Park Jezerka around the old Jezerka estate until 1949, by which time the tree had been standing on the slope for more than a century. It reaches 36 metres and grows beside the small pond fed by the estate's lower spring.

Its waistline is the one figure nobody has settled. Czech Wikipedia gives 473 centimetres and no date for the measurement. The Agentura Koniklec survey taped it at 517 in 2013. A Koniklec map from 2017 records 525. Those numbers do not so much contradict each other as catch one growth curve at three moments, and the tree is still working on it.

On the age the two sources agree: about 200 years as of 2016, so roughly 210 now. The estate building beside it was rebuilt as a chateau in 1835, when this plane was around twenty years old, and that same building now holds the Divadlo Na Jezerce theatre. Everything a visitor sees here except the tree and the spring arrived after it did.

Prague protected it as a pamatny strom on 8 February 2001, and the state rates its health very good. The park is free and open at any hour, which makes this the easiest of Prague's giants to walk up to and stand under.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size alone, a trunk over five metres round and 36 metres tall, older than everything around it. It stands beside the pond and its spring, between the theatre building and the water.

trees.name: The Oak of Na Cibulkach Forest Park

location.address: Lesopark Na Cibulkach (Prirodni park Kosire-Motol), south side of the path extending U Cibulky street near a crossroads, 150 00 Praha 5-Kosire

trees.access: Free, public forest park (Prirodni park Kosire-Motol, designated 1991), open at all times
trees.transport: Bus to Kosire, then a short walk into the Cibulka estate parkland
trees.story:
A crack runs up to eight metres down one side of this oak, and the conservation register still lists it as standing.

Prague's database has carried the tree since June 2007 and refreshed the entry in August 2024, hollow and vertical split and all. It went in around 1820, when the Cibulka estate above Kosire was being laid out as a landscape park. The estate house is a ruin today. The park outlived it and was made the Kosire-Motol nature park in 1991, which is how an oak planted for one family's private view ended up on public ground.

Neighbouring trees shade it and it has grown accordingly, upward rather than outward: a long straight trunk that forks into three branches high overhead and carries a narrow crown to 24 metres. Round the trunk it measures 408 centimetres, which is a serious oak anywhere else and the slimmer of the two here. Its registered neighbour 90 metres away, planted at about the same time, reaches 525.

The numbers say the crack has not finished it. A tape put round the trunk in 2011 read 394 centimetres; the register's 2024 update reads 408. Fourteen centimetres in thirteen years is a tree still laying down wood. Nobody has cored it, so the age is not a measurement: the register dates the planting to about 1820, which puts the tree near two centuries.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long straight trunk, 408 centimetres round and split by a long vertical crack, forking into three branches high overhead. It stands south of the path; the oak 90 metres away is barrel-shaped and much wider.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Oak with the Bizarre Trunk of Na Cibulkach

location.address: Lesopark Na Cibulkach (Prirodni park Kosire-Motol), at a Y-shaped fork of the path extending U Cibulky street, west of the housing estate across an unnamed stream, 150 00 Praha 5-Kosire

trees.access: Free, public forest park (Prirodni park Kosire-Motol, designated 1991), open at all times
trees.transport: Bus to Kosire, then a short walk into the Cibulka estate parkland; 90 metres from prg_022
trees.story:
Czech conservation law has an official name for this tree, and the name is the oak with the bizarre trunk.

It earns it. The trunk swells like a barrel, 525 centimetres round, then tapers and breaks into a crown so modest that the whole tree stops at 17 metres. Oaks that thick are usually far taller. This one put its two centuries into width.

It went into the ground around 1815, in the landscape park laid out at the Cibulka estate, and it has outlasted what it was planted for. The house above it is a ruin. The wood around it became the Kosire-Motol nature park in 1991, and Prague's register of protected trees added the oak itself in March 2008.

A survey in 2016 taped the trunk at 525 centimetres and the register's 2024 refresh carries the same number to the centimetre. That survey called the tree's condition deteriorated, which on an oak of this age describes a stage rather than an ending; the register still lists it as standing. Nobody has counted its rings, so the two centuries come from that planting date and should be read loosely.

Ninety metres away stands the park's other registered oak, taller, slimmer and cracked down one side. Seeing them within five minutes of each other is the argument for coming out to Kosire at all: same park, same decade, two completely different animals.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the barrel-shaped trunk, 525 centimetres round, tapering into a small crown only 17 metres up. It stands at the Y-shaped fork in the forest paths, west of the housing estate across the stream.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Beech of Brevnovska Gate, Hvezda

location.address: Obora Hvezda nature reserve, about 50 metres from the Brevnovska brana entrance (also called Vypisska or Prazska brana), on the main path toward the Hvezda summer palace, 162 00 Praha 6-Liboc

trees.access: Free, public nature reserve (Obora Hvezda), open year round
trees.transport: 10 min walk from the Obora Hvezda or Vypich tram and bus stops (same access as prg_005, about 230 metres away)
trees.story:
Two invading armies stripped this wood before the tree standing here was ever planted. French troops took the game reserve's timber during the War of the Austrian Succession, Prussian troops finished the work in the Seven Years' War, and after 1763 Hvezda was replanted with beech, oak and hornbeam. This beech is one of the oldest survivors of that replanting.

Assessments put it between 210 and 250 years old, revised to roughly 230 in 2019, so the arithmetic and the history agree with each other. It stands 50 metres inside the Brevnovska gate, on the main path toward the star-shaped Hvezda summer palace, and it is one of the tallest trees in the reserve: 34 metres when it was measured in 2009, with a crown 26 metres across and the heavy buttressed root flare that old beeches put down around their base.

It is also still growing. The trunk read 373 centimetres round in 2009, 380 in 2013 and 386 in the register's 2024 update. Its health was assessed as very good with no significant damage, which is not nothing for a tree of this age standing a step from the reserve's busiest path; the maintenance file recommends a safety prune for that same reason.

Do not confuse it with the twin beech 230 metres away near the same gate. Separate tree, separate register entry, and this is the one on the main path.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the heavy buttressed root flare under a trunk 386 centimetres round, and by its height, 34 metres, among the tallest here. It stands 50 metres inside the Brevnovska gate, beside the main path.
trees.notes: AOPK register kod 104291 (isop_id 52750), protected since 22 August 2001, last register update 2024-08-22 (still listed alive/publishable). One of the oldest beeches planted when the game reserve was restored and replanted with beech, oak and hornbeam sometime after 1763, following the destruction of the original stock first by French troops in the War of the Austrian Succession and then by Prussian troops in the Seven Years' War. Estimated age 210 to 250 years as of a 2016 assessment, revised to about 230 years in 2019; the same range this project already uses for prg_005 (The Twin Beech of Hvezda), a different, separately registered tree about 230 metres away near the same gate. Girth 373 cm (2009), 380 cm (2013), 386 cm per the register's 2024 update. Height 34 m in 2009, crown width 26 m, one of the tallest trees in the reserve. Health assessed very good in 2009 with no major visible damage; maintenance note recommends a safety/health pruning because it stands right beside the main path. Prominent buttressed root flare typical of old beeches. Stands about 50 metres inside the reserve from the Brevnovska gate, on the main path to the star-shaped Hvezda summer palace.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.name: The Oak of Libocka Gate, Hvezda

location.address: Obora Hvezda nature reserve, right of the main path from the Libocka brana entrance toward the Hvezda summer palace, past the group of horse chestnuts and just before the large children's playground built in 2019, 162 00 Praha 6-Liboc

trees.access: Free, public nature reserve (Obora Hvezda), open year round; Libocka gate reached from the Sidliste Petriny tram stop (lines 1 and 2) or on foot from Petriny metro station (line A)
trees.transport: Sidliste Petriny tram stop, short walk into the reserve via the Libocka gate
trees.story:
Prague's own conservation register cannot decide what this tree is. It has been listed since 2002 as a pedunculate oak, Quercus robur, but a 2015 update to the same register filed its data under Quercus petraea, the sessile oak, and the leaf photographs the register itself attaches are petiolate: stalked at the base, the sessile oak's diagnostic feature, not the pedunculate's near-stalkless leaf. Oak makes up 57 percent of the trees in the Hvezda reserve, nearly all of it pedunculate, and if the register's own photographs are read correctly, this crooked, gnarled specimen is the reserve's only individually registered sessile oak among them.

Whichever species it is, it has grown steadily since a formal survey first measured it in 2001, when its trunk read 345 centimetres round. By 2009 that had reached 352, and by 2013, 356, the figure the register still carries today. Assessors call its health excellent apart from a few dry branches and note it is actively maintained, which for an eighteen-metre tree with a sixteen-metre crown standing beside the reserve's busiest path is not surprising.

Nobody has cored it, so 175 years is an estimate rather than a count: the register put it near 165 in 2016. It has been protected since October 2002 and stands right of the main path from the Libocka gate toward the star-shaped Hvezda summer palace, past a stand of registered horse chestnuts and just before the reserve's playground.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crooked, gnarled branches and stalked leaves, unlike the reserve's other oaks, and a trunk 356 centimetres round. It stands right of the main path from the Libocka gate, past the horse chestnuts.

trees.name: The Oak on the Dam of Libocky Pond

location.address: On the northwest embankment (dam) of Libocky rybnik, between the bank and the footpath, Liboc, Prague 6

verified_sources: AOPK CR (Agentura ochrany prirody a krajiny CR) memorial-tree register, kod 104832, CC BY 4.0, https://gis.nature.cz/arcgis/rest/services/PamatneStromy/PamatneStromy/MapServer/1

https://cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seznam_pam%C3%A1tn%C3%BDch_strom%C5%AF_v_Praze (row for kod 104832, 'Dub na hrazi Libockeho rybnika', confirms species dub letni, location 'v polovine severozapadni hraze Libockeho rybnika mezi brehem a cestou' = 'in the middle of the NW dam of Libocky pond, between the bank and the path')
trees.access: Free, on a public footpath along the Libocky rybnik dam (Liboc / Divoka Sarka nature area, Prague 6); the 2017 revitalisation added stone steps and a rest platform on this dam. No gate, no ticket.
trees.transport: Tram lines 22, 25 or 58 to Vypich, then roughly 20-25 minutes on foot along the Divoka Sarka-Liboc path network to the pond's dam (about 1.5 km by straight-line map distance; not walked this pass, so treat the minutes as an estimate)
trees.story:
On paper this oak lost seven centimetres of waistline in nine years, which is not something living oaks do. A measurement taken in June 2015 put it at 424 centimetres round. The Czech nature agency's own 2024 update of the memorial-tree register says 417. Somebody remeasured, or somebody rounded, and the register's newer figure is the one carried here. Either way it is a big tree: more than four metres of trunk standing on the northwest dam of Libocky pond, between the water and the footpath, with nothing next to it competing for light.

That open position is why the state protected it on 13 July 2004. The designation cites its dominance and its typical pond-edge habit, and draws a circle of protection thirteen metres out from the trunk.

Nobody has dated it. Working from the girth and the growth rates Prague's other registered pedunculate oaks run at, a shade over two centimetres a year, it lands somewhere between 165 and 210 years old. That is an arithmetic answer rather than a measured one, and if anyone has a better figure we would like to hear it.

The dam itself was rebuilt in 2017, gaining stone steps and a wooden rest platform; people fish from the embankment. The oak came through the works and the last visit on record found it in very good health.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 417 centimetres round, standing clear of other trees halfway along the northwest dam of Libocky pond, between the water's edge and the path, near the stone steps built in 2017.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Beech Below the Summer Palace, Hvezda

location.address: In Obora Hvezda (the Hvezda game reserve), on the path descending from the Hvezda summer palace (Letohradek Hvezda) toward the Ruzynska gate, Liboc, Prague 6

verified_sources: AOPK CR memorial-tree register, kod 104281, CC BY 4.0, https://gis.nature.cz/arcgis/rest/services/PamatneStromy/PamatneStromy/MapServer/1

https://cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seznam_pam%C3%A1tn%C3%BDch_strom%C5%AF_v_Praze (row for kod 104281, 'Buk lesni pod letohradkem Hvezda', coordinates 50deg5'2"N 14deg19'29"E which convert to 50.0839,14.3247, matching the register point to within metres)
trees.access: Free, public nature reserve (Obora Hvezda), open year round, same regime as the three other Hvezda trees already published (prg_005, prg_024, prg_025)
trees.transport: Tram line 22 to Bila Hora, then a walk through Obora Hvezda toward the summer palace; exact walking distance from the tram stop not measured this pass (roughly 500 m by straight-line map distance from the reserve's edge)
trees.story:
This beech was protected for its height, not its age. When Prague listed it as a memorial tree on 9 September 2002, the reason given was that it is the tallest tree in the beech stand growing in this corner of Obora Hvezda: roughly 40 metres, on a trunk that stays straight almost the whole way up, with root buttresses flaring out where it meets the ground. The protection zone is a circle eleven metres out from the bark.

It is also one of the few trees here whose growing you can watch in the paperwork. The girth has been taken three times: 306 centimetres in the older listing, 332 in September 2013, 337 at the nature agency's 2024 update. Thirty centimetres of new wood in two decades, laid down while visitors walked past below it.

The age is softer than the measurements. The best any source offers is approximately 150 years, stated that loosely by the survey that recorded the 2013 girth, and it stays loose here rather than being tidied into a planting date. Add the years since and it is a little more.

It stands on the path most people take down from the Hvezda summer palace toward the Ruzynska gate. Two other beeches in the reserve carry the same protection and are easily confused with it; this is the one below the palace.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 40 metres and the tallest in this stand of beeches, on a trunk that runs straight most of the way up from flaring root buttresses. It stands on the path from the summer palace to the Ruzynska gate.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.name: The Oak Behind the Ranger's Lodge, Čimický háj

location.address: Čimický háj, behind the Čimická hájovna (forester's lodge), Praha 8-Bohnice

trees.story:
Two great oaks stand behind this forestry lodge and only one of them is still alive. This is the living one, and it is the smaller and younger of the pair. The other, where the path meets the lodge, is five metres round and about three hundred years old, and what is left of it is a hollow trunk carrying a thin ring of living crown at the top, an owl inside and a colony of bees; it keeps its protection as a habitat rather than as a living tree.

This oak is the one still putting on wood. It measured 3.55 metres round in 2011 and 3.81 when the register came back to it in August 2024, and it stands 32.5 metres tall, its crown carried upward rather than out. A 2013 survey put its age at about 180 years, which makes it roughly 190 now. Both trees were protected on the same day in 2004, and both sat for a portrait in 1969, when the painter Jaroslav Turek put the pair on one canvas. Only one of them has changed much since.

Čimický háj around them is working woodland that Bohnice and Kobylisy have turned into weekend ground, walked, run and cycled through all year, and the building in front of the tree is still a forestry lodge. That 2024 measurement is the newest hard record anyone has of this oak. If you get out there, tell us how it looks.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the healthy one of the two great oaks behind the forestry lodge: 3.81 metres round, with a full crown carried upward. Its neighbour is five metres round, hollow, and dead but for a ring of leaves at the top.
trees.access: Free, inside Čimický háj, a public recreational forest between Bohnice, Kobylisy and Čimice used year-round for walking, running and cycling. The tree stands a short way past a fence behind the Čimická hájovna (a working forestry lodge), which prazskestromy.cz's own access note does not flag as restricted; the lodge area carries information boards as a marked point of interest. No source states the tree itself is closed to visitors.
trees.transport: Bus stop "Čimický háj" (lines 102, 144, 152, 177, 200), on the forest edge

trees.name: The Oak of Pod Labuťkou Street

location.address: Pod Labuťkou street, opposite house no. 13, Praha 8-Libeň

trees.story:
In 2010 the Czech state drew a twelve-metre protected circle around a tree on a residential street in Libeň. This is it: an oak opposite number 13 on Pod Labuťkou, standing on ground that used to be a children's playground, under a slope grown over with scrub.

It is not a giant. The trunk came to 3.00 metres round in a 2016 survey and 3.14 when the register was updated in August 2024, and the tree reaches twenty metres. What it has is a shape street trees are almost never allowed to keep: a bushy crown whose lowest branches run all the way down to the ground, so the whole tree is one piece from the pavement up rather than a trunk with foliage parked on top. The same survey rated its health very good, noting a few dry branches and algae in the bark crevices, which is what the damp of this slope leaves on a trunk.

Its age is an estimate and not a record. The surveyors put it at about 170 years in 2016, so somewhere near 180 now. Beyond those two measurements and a short Czech account of them, almost nothing about this oak is written down anywhere. If you know more of its story, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, bushy and dropping its lowest branches right down to the ground, and by the trunk at 3.14 metres round. It stands on the slope side of Pod Labuťkou, opposite house number 13.
trees.access: Free, stands beside the public street Pod Labuťkou in Libeň, on the site of a former children's playground below a vegetated slope. An ordinary street tree, not inside any park or private grounds.
trees.transport: In Libeň, Praha 8; nearest tram/bus stops are in the surrounding Libeň streets (not pinned down to a single stop this pass)

trees.name: The Oak of Kobylisy

location.address: Park north of Střelničná street, Sídliště Ďáblice housing estate, Praha 8-Kobylisy

trees.story:
For its first century this oak stood inside a military shooting range. The Kobylisy range closed in 1938, the Ďáblice housing estate went up across the land afterwards, and the ground under the tree was turned into the estate's park. The oak stayed where it was and is now the largest thing in it.

A 2016 survey measured it at 3.80 metres round and 27 metres tall. The register came back in October 2024 with 4.36 metres, and the gap between those two numbers is wider than eight years of growth on its own explains, so read the waistline as the distance between two people with a tape rather than as a precise figure. By either of them it is a heavier trunk than the living oak behind the forestry lodge in Čimický háj, or the one on Pod Labuťkou down in Libeň, both of them a couple of kilometres from here.

The same surveyors dated its planting to around 1825, which puts it near two hundred years old, and it has the build of a tree given room: one straight sturdy stem, and above it a fan of branches all running upward. Protection came in January 2000 and takes in nineteen metres of ground in every direction from the trunk. Nothing more recent than that October 2024 measurement has been published about it, so the newest thing known about this oak is its waistline.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, straight and 4.36 metres round, under a fan of branches all reaching upward. It is the biggest tree by some way in the park north of Střelničná.
trees.access: Free, in a public park (the green space of the Sídliště Ďáblice housing estate) north of Střelničná street. An ordinary open park tree, no restrictions.
trees.transport: Kobylisy district, Praha 8; reachable from the Kobylisy or Střelničná tram/bus stops on the surrounding estate roads (not pinned to one specific stop this pass)
